section.name: Key Files and Force Field Selection in Force Field X (FFX)
section.p: This guide explains how FFX finds parameters, how to choose a force field, and how to use .key files to control simulations reproducibly.

subsection.name: Force field parameter sets
subsection.p: FFX ships with AMOEBA parameter sets. Common choices:

ul.li: Other AMOEBA variants may be available for small molecules, water, ions.
In a .key file in your working directory: forcefield AMOEBA_BIO_2018
Or via JVM property when launching ffxc with Maven: -Dforcefield=AMOEBA_BIO_2018.

subsection.p: FFX also reads parameter files listed by parameters lines in .key, or provided as XML/PRM files alongside structures.

subsection.name: What is a .key file?
subsection.p: A plain-text file named something.key in your run directory that sets defaults for all FFX commands. Typical entries:
subsection.source:
# Select force field forcefield AMOEBA_BIO_2018
# PME and cutoffs (override defaults if needed) # a-ewald 0.545 # ewald-cutoff 7.0 # vdw-cutoff 9.0 # polarization mutual
# Constraints/restraints examples (selection syntax in command docs) # restrain-distance 12 45 2.0 100.0 # freeze atom 1-100
subsection.p: Place the .key file in the same directory you run ffxc from. Commands will pick it up automatically.

ul.li: Explicit parameter files declared in .key (e.g., parameters my_smallmol.prm) augment or override base force-field values.
Provide small-molecule parameters via .prm/.xml and include them in .key with parameters <file>.
Check with ffxc Biotype and ffxc Energy to validate that all atoms are parameterized.
Keep a run.key under version control with your input structures.
Record FFX version and GPU/CPU platform in your logs; keep seeds fixed (e.g., --randomSeed for ion placement, and relevant MD seeds when available).
